hints: Let the indices run freely: increment `head` on every put and `tail` on every get, and never reduce them modulo `size`. Then `head - tail` is the number of stored bytes, and the physical slot is `index & (size - 1)`. Empty means `head == tail`, full means `head - tail == size`. No slot is wasted.

`uint16_t` operands are promoted to `int` before the subtraction, so `head - tail` can be **negative** after `head` wraps (`2 - 65534 = -65532`). Cast the difference back: `(uint16_t)(head - tail)`. That is arithmetic modulo 65 536, and it is exact because `size` divides 65 536. In `rb_read`, copy in at most two chunks: up to the physical end of the storage, then from slot 0.
explanation_md:
**Approach: free-running indices.** `head` counts every byte ever written and `tail` every byte ever read, both modulo 2^16. Then:

| quantity | expression |
|---|---|
| fill level | `(uint16_t)(head - tail)` |
| empty | `head == tail` |
| full | `(uint16_t)(head - tail) == size` |
| physical slot | `index & (size - 1)` |

Because `size` is a power of two that divides 65 536, the mapping `index & (size-1)` stays continuous when the 16-bit counters wrap, and the unsigned difference is exact as long as the fill level never exceeds 65 535. That gives the full capacity of `size` bytes without a `count` variable or a wasted slot.

**Why no count variable?** `count++` in the ISR and `count--` in the main loop are both read-modify-write sequences. If the ISR fires between the main loop's load and store, one update is lost. Fixing that needs a critical section, which adds interrupt latency. With split ownership (the ISR writes only `head`, the main loop writes only `tail`), every shared variable has exactly one writer. On a single core, with aligned 16-bit stores that are atomic, this is safe without locking.

**Ordering.** Write the data *before* publishing the new `head`, and read the data *before* publishing the new `tail`. `volatile` stops the compiler from caching or reordering the index accesses relative to each other. On a multi-core or weakly ordered CPU you would also need memory barriers (C11 `atomic_store_explicit(..., memory_order_release)`).

**Complexity.** `put`, `get`, `count`: O(1). `rb_read`: O(k), done as at most two `memcpy` calls. Space: `size` bytes plus two indices.

**Common mistakes**
- `if (rb->head - rb->tail == rb->size)`. Both operands are promoted to `int`, and after `head` wraps the difference is negative, so the FIFO never reports full and overwrites unread data. The `(uint16_t)` cast is essential.
- Reducing the indices with `% size` on every increment and then testing `head == tail`. Full and empty become indistinguishable. Classic fixes cost a slot or a flag; free-running indices cost nothing.
- Using `% size` with a size that is not a power of two together with free-running indices. The mapping jumps when the counter wraps at 65 536.
- Incrementing `head` before storing the byte. The main loop can then read a slot that has not been written yet.
- In `rb_read`, a single `memcpy` that runs past the physical end of the storage (the guard bytes catch it).

**Interview follow-ups**
- Make the buffer size arbitrary (not a power of two). (Indices wrap at `2 * size`, or keep one slot empty with `% size`.)
- Where exactly do you need a critical section if a **second** producer (e.g. a DMA half-transfer callback) is added?
- Replace the byte-wise ISR with DMA in circular mode: how do you compute `head` from the DMA's NDTR / remaining-count register?
- The ISR drops bytes when the buffer is full. How would you report the overrun to the application without a shared counter? (A producer-owned `overruns` counter that only the ISR increments.)

title: Sliding-Window Peak-to-Peak With Monotonic Deques
statement_md:
A bearing-wear monitor samples an accelerometer and computes the **peak-to-peak amplitude** (max minus min) over the last `k` samples, for every window position. A brute-force rescan of each window costs O(n*k), which is far too slow for `n = 10^6` samples and `k` up to `n`.

Implement

```c
void window_p2p(const int16_t *x, int n, int k, int32_t *out, int *work);
```

- For every `i` in `k-1 .. n-1`, write `out[i - k + 1] = max(x[i-k+1..i]) - min(x[i-k+1..i])`. That is `n - k + 1` outputs.
- `work` is caller-provided scratch space of **exactly `2 * k` ints**. Use it for your two deques. Do not use any other memory that grows with `n` or `k` (no static or global arrays, no `malloc`).
- The total time must be O(n), independent of `k`.

**How it is tested.** A hidden `main()` calls your function once. `work` is surrounded by guard words, so touching `work[2k]` or beyond is reported as `OUT OF BOUNDS WRITE`. Small tests print every output. Large generated tests compare with a reference and print `OK checksum=...`.

**Input (read by the hidden harness)**
- Either: line 1 `n k`, line 2 the `n` samples,
- or: one line `GEN n k seed`.

**Output**
- The `n - k + 1` peak-to-peak values on one line, or `OK checksum=X` / `WRONG at i`.

**Example**
```
Input:
8 3
1 3 -1 -3 5 3 6 7

Output:
4 6 8 8 3 4
```
Window `[-1 -3 5]` has max 5 and min -3, so its peak-to-peak value is 8.
constraints_md:
- `1 <= k <= n <= 1000000`
- `-32768 <= x[i] <= 32767` (`int16_t`), so a result can be up to 65535
- O(n) time, O(k) extra memory, only inside `work[0 .. 2k-1]`
hints: For the maximum, keep a deque of **indices** whose samples are strictly decreasing from front to back. Before pushing `i`, pop from the back every index whose sample is `<= x[i]`: those can never be the maximum again while `i` is in the window. The front is the current maximum. Drop it once it falls out of the window (`front <= i - k`). The minimum uses a mirrored deque.

At most `k` indices are alive at any time, so each deque fits in `k` ints if you store it as a **ring**: keep a head position and a length, and wrap positions with `if (p == k) p = 0;`. Expire the old front *before* pushing `i`. Then a deque never holds more than `k` entries. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, which gives O(n) in total.
explanation_md:
**Approach: two monotonic deques.** For the window maximum, keep candidate indices whose samples **strictly decrease** from front to back. When `x[i]` arrives, every back entry with `x[j] <= x[i]` is dominated: `i` is newer and at least as large, so `j` can never be a maximum again. Pop those and push `i`. The front is the window maximum; remove it once its index is `<= i - k`. The minimum deque is the mirror image. Peak-to-peak is `x[front_max] - x[front_min]`.

```
x = 1 3 -1 -3 5 ...   k = 3
i=2 max-dq [3,-1]      min-dq [-1]       -> 3 - (-1) = 4
i=3 max-dq [3,-1,-3]   min-dq [-3]       -> 6
i=4 max-dq [5]         min-dq [-3,5]     -> 8
```

**O(k) memory in a fixed buffer.** The live indices always lie in `(i-k, i]`, so each deque holds at most `k` entries. If the expired front is removed **before** the push, the deque never exceeds `k`. That is why it can be a ring of exactly `k` ints. A deque that only grows to the right would need `n` slots.

**Complexity.** Time O(n) amortised: each index is pushed once and popped at most once per deque, whatever `k` is. Space O(k), in `work`.

**Common mistakes**
- Storing **values** instead of indices. You then cannot tell when the front has left the window, especially with duplicates.
- Expiring after the push. The deque briefly holds `k + 1` entries and writes `work[2k]`, which the guard catches.
- Using `<` instead of `<=` when popping (or the reverse in the min deque). It is still correct, but duplicates pile up; with `k = n` and constant input the ring overflows its `k` slots if expiry is also late.
- `int16_t` result: `32767 - (-32768) = 65535` does not fit. Widen before subtracting.
- O(n*k) rescans: for `k = 500 000` that is 5 * 10^11 operations.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Return the **longest** window whose peak-to-peak stays below a threshold (two pointers plus the same two deques).
- A streaming version for an ISR: one sample in, one p2p value out, O(1) amortised. What is the worst-case time of a single call, and why does that matter for interrupt latency? (The back-pop loop can take O(k) once.)
- Compare with a van Herk/Gil-Werman block algorithm (3 comparisons per sample, worst-case bounded) for hard real-time use.
- How do you extend this to a **sliding median**? (Two heaps or an order-statistic structure; see the median-filter question.)

title: NTC Calibration Lookup Table With Linear Interpolation
statement_md:
An NTC thermistor's resistance is not linear in temperature, so the ECU converts the raw ADC value with a **calibration table** stored in flash. The table has breakpoints `x[i]` (ADC counts, **strictly increasing**) and values `y[i]` (temperature in 0.1 degC). `y` may rise or fall; for an NTC it falls.

```c
typedef struct {
    const uint16_t *x;   /* breakpoints, strictly increasing */
    const int16_t  *y;   /* output at each breakpoint        */
    uint16_t        n;   /* number of breakpoints, 1..4096   */
} lut_t;

int16_t lut_interp(const lut_t *t, uint16_t adc);
```

Rules:
- `adc <= x[0]` returns `y[0]`, and `adc >= x[n-1]` returns `y[n-1]` (**clamp**, never extrapolate).
- Otherwise find the segment `x[i] <= adc < x[i+1]` and return
  `y[i] + round( (y[i+1] - y[i]) * (adc - x[i]) / (x[i+1] - x[i]) )`,
  where `round` goes to the **nearest integer, with exact halves rounded away from zero** (`2.5 -> 3`, `-2.5 -> -3`).
- **Integer arithmetic only.** The target MCU has no FPU.
- Find the segment in **O(log n)**: the harness makes up to 10^6 lookups in a 4096-entry table.
- `y` spans the full `int16_t` range and `x` the full `uint16_t` range, so `(y[i+1]-y[i]) * (adc-x[i])` can reach about 4.3 * 10^9. The judge runs with UBSan.

**How it is tested.** A hidden `main()` builds the table at the very **end** of a buffer (reading past `x[n-1]` or `y[n-1]` is out of bounds) and prints one result per query. Generated tests compare against a reference and print `OK checksum=...`.

**Input (read by the hidden harness)**
- Either: `n`, then `n` lines `x y`, then `q`, then `q` lines `adc`,
- or: one line `GEN n q seed`.

**Example**
```
Input:
6
200 1250
500 800
1000 450
2000 250
3000 50
3800 -300
4
100
350
505
4095

Output:
1250
1025
796
-300
```
`505`: `800 + round(-350 * 5 / 500) = 800 + round(-3.5) = 800 - 4 = 796`.
constraints_md:
- `1 <= n <= 4096`, `x` strictly increasing in `0..65535`, `y` in `-32768..32767`
- `1 <= q <= 1000000`, `0 <= adc <= 65535`
- O(log n) per lookup, integer arithmetic only, no writes to the table
hints: Clamp first. Then binary-search the segment with the invariant `x[lo] <= adc < x[hi]`, starting from `lo = 0`, `hi = n - 1`. Loop while `hi - lo > 1`, so `mid` is always strictly inside and `lo = mid` cannot stall.

Do the interpolation in `int64_t`: `num = (int64_t)(y1 - y0) * (adc - x0)`, `den = x1 - x0 > 0`. Round half away from zero without floating point: `num >= 0 ? (2*num + den) / (2*den) : -((-2*num + den) / (2*den))`. Plain `/` truncates toward zero, so a separate case for negative values is needed.
explanation_md:
**Approach.**
1. **Clamp** outside the table. Extrapolating an NTC curve beyond its last breakpoint gives absurd temperatures, and an open or shorted sensor would then look like a plausible value.
2. **Binary search** for the segment with the invariant `x[lo] <= adc < x[hi]`. Because the loop runs only while `hi - lo > 1`, `mid` is strictly between them, so both `lo = mid` and `hi = mid` make progress. O(log n): 12 steps for 4096 breakpoints instead of up to 4096.
3. **Interpolate in 64 bits.** `dy` can be ±65 535 and `dx` up to 65 535, so the product reaches 4.29 * 10^9, more than `INT32_MAX`. On a 32-bit MCU an `int32_t` multiply silently wraps (it is formally UB); the result is a wrong temperature only in certain segments.
4. **Round correctly.** C's `/` truncates toward zero, so `-3.5` becomes `-3` and `3.5` becomes `3`. Rounding half away from zero needs the sign split shown above (`2*num + den` over `2*den`).

```
adc = 505 in [500, 1000]: dy = -350, dx = 5, den = 500
num = -1750 -> -((3500 + 500) / 1000) = -4 -> 800 - 4 = 796
```

**Complexity.** O(log n) per lookup, O(1) extra memory. The table is read-only and can stay `const` in flash.

**Common mistakes**
- `int32_t` (or `int`) product: overflows for steep, wide segments (sample 2 with `adc = 40000`).
- `(dy * dx + den / 2) / den` for all signs: rounds negative values the wrong way (`-3.5 -> -3`).
- Linear search: correct, but 4096 * 10^6 comparisons is too slow here and wastes CPU in a 1 ms task.
- Binary search off-by-one: returning `hi` as the segment start, or reading `x[i+1]` when `adc == x[n-1]`, which is one past the table (the harness places the table at the end of its buffer, so ASan reports it).
- Extrapolating instead of clamping.
- Dividing first (`dy / dx * (adc - x0)`): precision is lost; for `|dy| < dx` the slope truncates to 0.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Uniformly spaced breakpoints (`x[i] = x0 + i * 2^s`): the segment index is `(adc - x0) >> s` and the division becomes a shift. Why do most calibration tables in production use this layout?
- Make the table **monotonic-safe**: what should happen if a calibration engineer flashes a table whose `x` is not strictly increasing? (Check at start-up and report a DTC; `den == 0` would otherwise divide by zero.)
- Inverse lookup: given a temperature, find the ADC threshold for a fan-on comparator. (Binary search on `y`, which is monotonic decreasing for an NTC.)
- 2D maps (e.g. ignition timing over RPM x load): bilinear interpolation with two binary searches.

title: De-interleave a DMA Audio Buffer In Place (Cycle-Leader Transpose)
statement_md:
A multi-channel ADC (e.g. a microphone array for in-cabin noise cancellation) writes samples by DMA in **interleaved** order: frame 0 of every channel, then frame 1 of every channel, and so on. The DSP library needs **planar** order: all frames of channel 0, then all frames of channel 1, ...

```
interleaved (F = 3 frames, C = 2 channels):  L0 R0 L1 R1 L2 R2
planar:                                       L0 L1 L2 R0 R1 R2
```

This is an in-place **transpose** of an `F x C` row-major matrix into a `C x F` one. The buffer fills most of the SRAM, so there is **no room for a copy**, and not even for a "visited" bitmap: only O(1) extra memory (a few scalar variables).

Implement

```c
void deinterleave(int16_t *buf, int frames, int channels);
```

After the call, `buf[c * frames + f]` must hold the sample that was at `buf[f * channels + c]`.

**How it is tested.** A hidden `main()` calls your function once. Guard words around the buffer detect out-of-bounds writes. Small tests print the planar result one channel per line. Large generated tests (up to 2^20 samples) are compared with the original and print `OK` or `WRONG`.

**Input (read by the hidden harness)**
- Either: line 1 `F C`, then `F` lines of `C` samples (one frame per line),
- or: one line `GEN F C seed`.

**Output**
- `chK: s0 s1 ...` for each channel, or `OK` / `WRONG at channel c frame f`.

**Example**
```
Input:
3 2
1 10
2 20
3 30

Output:
ch0: 1 2 3
ch1: 10 20 30
```
constraints_md:
- `1 <= F, C` and `F * C <= 1048576`
- Samples are `int16_t`
- O(1) extra memory. Expected time about O(N log N) for `N = F * C` (the cycle-leader method); it must finish in the time limit for every shape.
hints: Index the buffer linearly with `N = F * C`. The sample at position `i = f*C + c` must move to `j = c*F + f`. Positions `0` and `N-1` never move. For every other `i` you can show that `j = (i * F) mod (N - 1)`. So the transpose is a **permutation** made of disjoint cycles.

Rotate each cycle exactly once, carrying one sample along it with a single temporary. Without a visited bitmap, decide whether `s` should start (lead) a cycle by walking `next(s), next(next(s)), ...`. If you meet an index smaller than `s` first, that cycle was already rotated from its smallest member, so skip `s`. If you come back to `s`, rotate the cycle now. Use 64-bit arithmetic for `i * F`.
explanation_md:
**Approach: follow the permutation's cycles.** In the flat buffer the sample at `i = f*C + c` must go to `j = c*F + f`. Since `N = F*C ≡ 1 (mod N-1)`:

```
i * F = f*C*F + c*F = f*N + c*F ≡ f + c*F = j   (mod N-1)
```

So `next(i) = i*F mod (N-1)` for `0 < i < N-1`, and `0` and `N-1` are fixed points. The permutation splits into disjoint cycles. Rotating one cycle needs only a single carried sample:

```
F=3, C=2, N-1 = 5, next(i) = 3i mod 5:   1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1
R0 (pos 1) -> pos 3, R1 (pos 3) -> pos 4, L2 (pos 4) -> pos 2, L1 (pos 2) -> pos 1
L0 R0 L1 R1 L2 R2   ->   L0 L1 L2 R0 R1 R2
```

**No bitmap: the cycle-leader test.** Rotate each cycle only from its **smallest** index. For a candidate `s`, walk the cycle: meeting an index `< s` means the cycle was handled already, and returning to `s` means `s` is the leader. This uses O(1) memory; the price is extra walking. In practice the total work is about O(N log N), which is fast enough for a 1M-sample buffer.

**Complexity.** Time: each cycle is rotated once (N moves in total) plus the leader walks, about O(N log N) in practice and O(N^2) in the worst theoretical case. Space O(1). A visited bitmap (N bits, 128 KB here) would give O(N), but it is not available.

**Common mistakes**
- Using an `F x C` scratch copy. It is trivially correct, but it doubles the RAM, which is exactly what the problem forbids.
- Forgetting that `N - 1` is the modulus (not `N`), and not special-casing `N < 3` (modulo by 0 when `N == 1`).
- Overflow in `i * F` with 32-bit math: `1 048 575 * 524 288` does not fit in 32 bits.
- Rotating every cycle once per member: each cycle is rotated many times, which scrambles the data.
- Swapping `buf[i]` with `buf[next(i)]` in a loop over `i`. Pairwise swaps only work for square matrices.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Prove that `i*F mod (N-1)` is the inverse of `i*C mod (N-1)`. Which one re-interleaves planar data for the DAC?
- With a few hundred bytes of scratch, how would you speed this up? (Block transposes; or a small bitmap of already-processed cycle leaders.)
- Avoid the problem entirely: configure the DMA with a **channel stride** (scatter mode) or use two DMA streams so the data lands planar. What hardware features do STM32/TI DSP DMA controllers offer for this?
- For `C = 2` (stereo), a simpler O(N log N) recursive "perfect shuffle" exists. Sketch it.

title: Lowest Free Handle ID in O(n) Time and O(1) Memory
statement_md:
A diagnostic server hands out session handles `1, 2, 3, ...`. When a new tester connects, it must get the **smallest positive ID that is not in use**. The list of IDs in use is collected from several modules, so it is messy. It can contain duplicates, `0`, negative error codes, `INT_MIN`, and IDs far above the list length.

Implement

```c
int lowest_free_id(int *ids, int n);
```

It returns the smallest integer `>= 1` that does not occur in `ids[0..n-1]`.

- O(n) time and **O(1) extra memory**. There is no RAM for a "seen" table of size `n`.
- The array is a scratch copy, so you **may reorder or overwrite** it.
- `ids` may be `NULL` only when `n == 0` (then the answer is `1`).
- `qsort` is disabled. Sorting is O(n log n) anyway.

**How it is tested.** A hidden `main()` calls your function once and prints the result. Large tests (up to 10^6 IDs) are generated by the harness and checked against a reference.

**Input (read by the hidden harness)**
- Either: line 1 `n`, line 2 the `n` IDs,
- or: one line `GEN n seed holes`. The harness takes `1..n`, replaces `holes` random entries by junk (0, negative, too large, duplicates, `INT_MIN`/`INT_MAX`) and shuffles.

**Output**
- The lowest free ID.

**Example**
```
Input:
5
3 4 -1 1 7

Output:
2
```
constraints_md:
- `0 <= n <= 1000000`
- `INT_MIN <= ids[i] <= INT_MAX`
- O(n) time, O(1) extra memory; modifying `ids` is allowed.
hints: The answer is always in `1 .. n+1`: `n` values cannot cover more than `1..n`. So only the values in `[1, n]` matter, and the array itself has exactly `n` slots that can serve as a "seen" table: slot `v - 1` for value `v`.

**Cyclic placement:** for each `i`, while `ids[i] = v` lies in `[1, n]` and `ids[v-1] != v`, swap `ids[i]` with `ids[v-1]`. Then scan for the first `i` with `ids[i] != i + 1`. Test `ids[v-1] != v` (not `ids[i] != i+1`), or duplicates loop forever. Check the range **before** computing `v - 1`, because `INT_MIN - 1` overflows.
explanation_md:
**Approach: use the array as its own hash table (cyclic sort).** The answer lies in `1..n+1`, so every value outside `[1, n]` is irrelevant. Value `v` in range "belongs" in slot `v - 1`. Swap values home until each slot holds its own number or junk:

```
3 4 -1 1 7      i=0: 3 -> slot 2   -1 4 3 1 7
                i=1: 4 -> slot 3   -1 1 3 4 7
                     1 -> slot 0    1 -1 3 4 7
scan: slot 1 holds -1 -> answer 2
```

**Why O(n).** Every swap puts at least one value into its final slot, where it stays (`ids[v-1] == v` stops further moves). So there are at most `n` swaps in total, even though there is a `while` inside the `for`.

**Termination with duplicates.** The guard `ids[v-1] != v` stops the loop when the home slot already holds a copy of `v`. The tempting guard `ids[i] != i + 1` spins forever on `1 1`: it keeps swapping the two equal values.

**Complexity.** Time O(n), at most `n` swaps plus two scans. Extra space O(1). (Alternative: the sign-marking trick, which first replaces junk by `n + 1` and then marks seen values by negating `ids[v-1]`. Also O(1), but it needs care with `INT_MIN`.)

**Common mistakes**
- Sorting (O(n log n)) or a `seen[n + 1]` table (O(n) RAM). Both are correct, but they break the constraints.
- `ids[ids[i] - 1]` evaluated before the range check. `INT_MIN - 1` is signed overflow (UB), and a large value indexes far outside the array.
- The swap written as `ids[i] = ids[ids[i]-1]; ids[ids[i]-1] = v;`. The second index is computed from the **already overwritten** `ids[i]`. Save `v` first and index with `v - 1`.
- Returning `n` instead of `n + 1` when `1..n` are all present.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Do it **without modifying** the array, in O(n) time and O(1) memory. (Not possible in general; discuss bitmaps of n bits, or O(n log n) with binary search on the answer by counting.)
- Handles are released and re-allocated all the time. Design an O(1) allocator instead. (A free list threaded through a fixed array, or a bitmap with find-first-zero using `__builtin_ctz`.)
- The IDs are 8-bit and the table is at most 255 entries. What simpler, faster solution do you use on an 8-bit MCU? (A 32-byte bitmap.)

title: Stuck-Sensor and Short-Circuit Detection Across ADC Channels
statement_md:
An ECU samples `C` analog sensor channels (12-bit, `0..4095`) every cycle. Each **frame** holds one sample per channel. A plausibility monitor must detect two fault types per channel and report when they appear and disappear.

**Runs.** For every channel, consecutive samples form a *run*. The first sample of a run is its **anchor** `a`. A new sample `x` **continues** the run if:
- `a` is a rail value (`0` or `4095`): `x == a` exactly;
- otherwise: `x` is **not** a rail value and `|x - a| <= T`. The comparison is against the **anchor**, not the previous sample, so a slow drift does *not* count as stuck.

If `x` does not continue the run, a new run starts at `x`. The first frame always starts a run.

**Faults** (at most one per run, raised in the frame where the run reaches the threshold):
- a non-rail run reaching length `K`: `f=<frame> ch=<c> STUCK since f=<start> value=<anchor>`
- a run at `0` reaching length `R`: `f=<frame> ch=<c> SHORT_GND since f=<start>`
- a run at `4095` reaching length `R`: `f=<frame> ch=<c> SHORT_BAT since f=<start>`

When a run that raised a fault ends (a new run starts in frame `f`): `f=<f> ch=<c> CLEARED after <len> frames`. This line comes before any fault raised by the new run in the same frame. Events are printed frame by frame, and within a frame by channel `0..C-1`.

After the last frame, print `END ch=<c> <TYPE> active, <len> frames` for every channel whose current run holds a fault (in channel order), then `summary: <n> faults` (the number of faults raised).

**Input**
- Line 1: `C N K R T`.
- Next `N` lines: `C` samples each.

**Example**
```
Input:
1 10 4 2 0
100
100
100
100
100
101
0
0
0
50

Output:
f=3 ch=0 STUCK since f=0 value=100
f=5 ch=0 CLEARED after 5 frames
f=7 ch=0 SHORT_GND since f=6
f=9 ch=0 CLEARED after 3 frames
summary: 2 faults
```
constraints_md:
- `1 <= C <= 8`, `1 <= N <= 100000`
- `1 <= R <= 1000000`, `1 <= K <= 1000000` (thresholds may exceed `N`)
- `0 <= T <= 4095`, `0 <= sample <= 4095`
- O(N * C) time, O(C) memory: process frames as they arrive, do not store the whole recording.

summary: 50 faults

hints: Keep one small struct per channel, `{anchor, start, len, fault}`, in an array indexed by the channel number. Each sample either extends that channel's run or starts a new one. The whole recording never needs to be stored.

Order matters inside a frame: (1) decide whether the run continues; (2) if not, print `CLEARED` for the old run if it had a fault, then reset the run to `{x, f, 1, none}`; (3) if the run has no fault yet, test `len == R` (rail anchor) or `len == K` (other anchor). Testing with `==` raises each fault exactly once, in the frame where the threshold is reached.
explanation_md:
**Approach: one run-length state machine per channel.** The state of a channel is `{anchor, start, len, fault}`, stored in an array of structs indexed by channel. For every sample:
1. **Continue or restart.** Rails need an exact match. Other values must stay within `T` of the **anchor**. A "within `T` of the previous sample" rule would call a slow, legitimate drift (e.g. coolant warming up) stuck, because every step is small.
2. **On restart**, report `CLEARED` if the old run had a fault, then reset the state.
3. **Raise once.** `len == K` (or `== R` for rails) is true in exactly one frame per run, so there is no separate "already reported" flag and no repeated events. The `fault` field records it for `CLEARED`/`END`.

Rails get their own, usually shorter, threshold `R`. A reading pinned at 0 V or Vref is the typical signature of a short to ground or to battery (or an open circuit with a pull-up/pull-down), and must be reported faster than a "frozen" mid-range value, which needs more evidence.

**Complexity.** Time O(N * C): constant work per sample. Memory O(C): the recording is never stored, as in a real ECU, where samples stream in from the ADC every cycle.

**Common mistakes**
- Comparing with the previous sample instead of the anchor (the drift test then reports a false STUCK).
- Letting a value within `T` of a mid-range anchor continue the run when it is a rail value (`3 -> 0` with `T = 5`). A short circuit would then hide inside a STUCK run.
- `len >= K` without the fault guard: the fault is reported on every frame. `len > K`: an off-by-one, one frame late.
- Printing `CLEARED` for runs that never raised a fault, or printing it *after* the new run's fault in the same frame (`K = 1`).
- A single global state instead of one per channel: channels corrupt each other.
- Forgetting the `END` lines for faults that are still active when the data stops.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Real DTC handling uses **debounce counters** (AUTOSAR DEM: `+step` on failed, `-step` on passed, thresholds for PREFAILED/FAILED). How would you map these runs onto a counter-based debounce?
- The ADC noise floor is 2 LSB, but a stuck sensor reads *exactly* the same value. Which `T` would you choose, and what about a sensor whose genuine signal is constant (e.g. a parked vehicle)? (Cross-check with a correlated signal: speed vs. wheel-speed sensors.)
- Store this state for 64 channels in an 8-bit MCU with 256 bytes of RAM: which field widths would you pick, and how do you saturate `len`?
- How would you test the monitor itself in production (fault injection)?

title: Walking a 2D Sensor Grid Through Row 0
constraints_md:
- Platform: x86-64 Linux, gcc, C11.
- The memory layout claim in the statement is true. The question is what the C standard says about the access.
hints: `grid[0]` is not "the grid". It is an object of type `int[4]`. What does the standard say about a subscript beyond the bounds of the array you are indexing, even if other valid memory happens to be there?

C11 Annex J.2 lists this exact case as undefined: *"An array subscript is out of range, even if an object is apparently accessible with the given subscript (as in the lvalue expression `a[1][7]` given the declaration `int a[4][5]`)"*. `grid[0][4]` through `grid[0][11]` are out of range.
explanation_md:
**Answer: `Undefined Behavior`.**

`grid[0][k]` means `*(grid[0] + k)`. `grid[0]` is an array of **4** `int`s. It decays to a pointer to its first element, and pointer arithmetic is defined only within that array (and one past its end, which may not be dereferenced), per C11 6.5.6p8. For `k >= 4` the access is outside the `int[4]` object, even though the memory belongs to `grid[1]`. Annex J.2 names this case explicitly (`a[1][7]` for `int a[4][5]`).

**What really happens.**
- At `-O0` without sanitizers, gcc usually prints `78`, the "expected" sum. That is why the bug survives code review and bench tests.
- With the judge's UBSan, `-fsanitize=bounds` stops the program at `k = 4`: *index 4 out of bounds for type 'int [4]'*.
- At `-O2`, gcc can assume the loop body never runs with `k >= 4` (`-Waggressive-loop-optimizations`). It may cut the loop short or produce an infinite loop. This broke the SPEC CPU2006 benchmark `h264ref` when gcc 4.8 introduced this optimisation.

**Correct ways to flatten.**
- Nested loops over `r` and `c` (the compiler generates the same linear walk anyway).
- Declare the storage as one flat array `int flat[ROWS * COLS]` and index it with `r * COLS + c`.
- `(int *)grid` walked to 12 elements is widely used and works with every mainstream compiler, but its strict conformance is debated. MISRA C forbids it (Rule 18.1), so do not rely on it in safety code.

**Complexity.** N/A (a correctness question); the defined versions are O(R * C) like the original.

**Common mistakes**
- Answering `78`. That is one possible behavior of UB, not the defined result.
- Believing "contiguous memory" makes the access legal. The rules are about the **object** being indexed, not about the addresses.
- Thinking sanitizers or `-O0` behavior prove the code correct.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Is `&grid[0][4]` (without dereferencing) allowed? (Yes: one past the end of `grid[0]`. But `&grid[0][5]` is already UB.)
- How do you pass this grid to a function so that the callee can index `[r][c]` correctly? (`int (*g)[4]`, or a VLA parameter `int g[][cols]`.)
- Why might a static analyser (Polyspace, Coverity, MISRA checker) flag `memcpy(dst, grid[0], sizeof grid)` but not `memcpy(dst, grid, sizeof grid)`?

title: Pointer-to-Row Arithmetic and sizeof on a VLA Type
constraints_md:
- Platform: x86-64 Linux, gcc, C11 (variable length arrays supported).
- Every access stays inside the row it indexes; the snippet has no undefined behavior.
hints: `m + 1` has type `int (*)[4]`: it points at the whole row `m[1]`. Postfix operators bind tighter than unary ones, so `-1[q]` is `-(1[q])`, which is `-(q[1])`.

`sizeof` normally does **not** evaluate its operand. The exception (C11 6.5.3.4p2) is an operand of **variable length array** type: then the size expression is evaluated at run time, with its side effects.
explanation_md:
**Answer:**
```
3 16 8
5 -11 8
11 12
32 4 3
```

**Line 1.** `sizeof m = 3*4*4 = 48` and `sizeof m[0] = 16`, so there are 3 rows. `p` is a pointer to a 4-int row, so `*p` is a whole row (16 bytes). `p + 0` is a pointer (8).

**Line 2.** `p = m + 1` points at row 1, so `**p = m[1][0] = 5` and `(*p)[3] = m[1][3] = 8`. `q` points at `m[2][1]`. Subscripting is a **postfix** operator, which binds tighter than unary minus, so `-1[q]` parses as `-(1[q]) = -(q[1]) = -m[2][2] = -11`. It is not `(-1)[q]`, which would be `q[-1] = m[2][0]`.

**Line 3.** `p[1]` is `*(p + 1)`, which is row `m[2]`, so `p[1][2] = 11`. `*(m + 2)` is also row `m[2]`; it decays to `&m[2][0]`, `+ 3` gives `&m[2][3]`, so the value is 12. Every access stays inside the row being indexed, so all of this is well defined.

**Line 4.** `sizeof` is usually a compile-time constant and its operand is **not evaluated**: `sizeof(n++)` is `sizeof(int) = 4`, and `n` does not change. The one exception is a **variable length array type** (C11 6.5.3.4p2): `int[n++][4]` has a run-time size, so `n++` *is* evaluated. The size uses the old value `2` (2 * 4 * 4 = 32), and `n` becomes 3.

**Complexity.** N/A. Only the VLA `sizeof` costs anything at run time (a multiply).

**Common mistakes**
- Treating `p + 1` like `int *` arithmetic (4 bytes) instead of a whole row (16 bytes).
- Reading `-1[q]` as `q[-1]`. Precedence: postfix `[]` before unary `-`.
- Assuming every `sizeof` is side-effect-free. With VLAs it is not, which is one reason MISRA C:2012 (Rule 18.8) bans VLAs, and Rule 13.6 forbids side effects in `sizeof` operands.
- Putting `n` and `sizeof(int[n++][4])` in the **same** `printf` call. The read of `n` and the side effect would be unsequenced, which is UB (C11 6.5p2). That is why the snippet uses separate statements.

**Interview follow-ups**
- Why are VLAs dangerous on a microcontroller even when they are used correctly? (Unbounded stack use, no failure reporting, and C11 made them optional, `__STDC_NO_VLA__`.)
- Declare a function parameter that receives `m` and allows `g[r][c]` indexing: `void f(int rows, int g[][4])` versus `void f(int rows, int cols, int g[rows][cols])`.
- What are the types of `m`, `m[0]`, `&m`, `&m[0]` and `*m`, and how many bytes does each advance on `+ 1` (after decay)? (`m`: 16, `m[0]`: 4, `&m`: 48, `&m[0]`: 16, `*m`: 4.)

title: Median Filter That Corrupts Its Own Sample History
statement_md:
A wheel-speed sensor occasionally produces single-sample spikes (EMI from the ignition). A **5-tap median filter** removes them: each output is the median of the last 5 samples. During the warm-up (fewer than 5 samples so far) it is the **lower median** of the samples received so far, i.e. element `(count - 1) / 2` of them in sorted order.

The window is kept in a small circular buffer `win[5]` with a write index `idx`. The first five outputs are always right. After that the filter sometimes lets a spike through or returns a value that is not in the last five samples at all, and on a constant signal with one spike it can stay wrong for several cycles.

Find and fix the bug. Do not change the input or output format.

**Input**
- Line 1: `n`. Line 2: `n` samples (`int16_t`).

**Output**
- The `n` filtered values on one line.

**Example**
```
Input:
7
10 50 20 40 30 1000 35

Output:
10 10 20 20 30 40 35
```
The 7th output is the median of `20 40 30 1000 35`, which is `35`.
constraints_md:
- `1 <= n <= 100000`
- `-32768 <= sample <= 32767`
- Window length 5, lower median during warm-up.
hints: What does `win` look like **after** `median_update` returns? Write it down for the example after the 5th sample, then follow which slot the 6th and 7th samples overwrite.

`int16_t *v = m->win;` does not copy anything: `v` **aliases** the history, so sorting `v` reorders the circular buffer. After that, `win[idx]` is no longer the oldest sample, and the filter evicts the wrong value. Sort a **local copy** of the window instead.
explanation_md:
**Bug.** `int16_t *v = m->win;` creates a second **name** for the history buffer, not a copy. `sort_i16(v, ...)` therefore sorts the circular buffer itself. The buffer's meaning ("slot `idx` holds the oldest sample") depends on the *age order* of its slots, and sorting replaces age order with value order. From the 6th sample on, `win[idx]` is just "whatever value ended up in that slot", so the filter evicts a random sample instead of the oldest one:

```
after 5 samples (sorted in place): win = 10 20 30 40 50, idx = 0
6th sample 1000 overwrites win[0] (10, which happens to be the oldest) -> 40, correct by luck
   ...and the sort turns win into 20 30 40 50 1000, idx = 1
7th sample 35 overwrites win[1] = 30 (but the oldest is 50!) -> 20 35 40 50 1000 -> 40, should be 35
```

During warm-up the bug is invisible: the free slots are always at the end, so sorting the filled prefix does no harm. That is why the first five outputs are always right.

**Fix.** Copy the window into a local array and sort the copy (10 bytes of stack here). The history keeps its circular age order.

**Complexity.** O(W^2) per sample with insertion sort on W = 5 values (at most 10 comparisons), O(W) extra stack. For large windows use a sorted array updated with one delete and one insert (O(W)), or two heaps (O(log W)).

**Common mistakes**
- Assuming pointer assignment copies an array. In C only `memcpy`, a loop, or struct assignment copy data; `v = m->win` just aliases it.
- Fixing the symptom by re-sorting the window "back" in some order. The age information is already lost.
- Taking the median of all 5 slots during warm-up (including the zero-initialised ones), which pulls the first outputs toward 0.
- `(m->count - 1) / 2` with `count == 0` would underflow; it cannot happen here because `count` is incremented first.

**Interview follow-ups**
- For a 3-tap median, write a branch-only version with no sorting (`max(min(a,b), min(max(a,b), c))`). How many comparisons does it need?
- Median vs. moving average for spike rejection: what happens to a step change, and to a single 32767 spike, in each filter?
- Implement an O(W) per-sample median for W = 31 that keeps a second, sorted array alongside the circular buffer: remove the evicted value (binary search) and insert the new one.
- Why can a median filter be unsuitable for a control loop's feedback signal? (Non-linear, so no transfer function; variable group delay.)

title: Pre-Trigger Snapshot From a Circular Sample Buffer
statement_md:
A crash data recorder samples a sensor continuously into a **circular buffer of 32 samples**. When a trigger fires (e.g. airbag deployment), it must freeze the last `P` samples **up to and including the trigger sample**, oldest first, so that engineers can see what happened just before the event. If fewer than `P` samples have been recorded since power-up, it freezes all of them.

The code works on the bench for the first trigger. In vehicle tests, some later triggers deliver garbage or crash the logger task, depending on **when** the trigger arrives relative to the buffer wrap-around. Under the judge, those cases are reported as an out-of-bounds access.

Find and fix the bug. Do not change the input or output format.

**Input**
- Line 1: `P n`, the pre-trigger length and the number of samples.
- Line 2: the `n` samples in time order.
- Line 3: `k` followed by `k` trigger positions `t` (strictly increasing). A trigger at `t` fires right after sample `t` (0-based) has been logged.

**Output**
- For each trigger: `trigger at t: s s s ...`, the frozen samples oldest first.

**Example**
```
Input:
5 40
100 101 102 ... 139   (the 40 values 100..139)
1 33

Output:
trigger at 33: 129 130 131 132 133
```

hidden_tests.output:
trigger at 0: -32768
trigger at 1: 32767
trigger at 2: 0

hints: Evaluate `start` by hand for the example: after 34 samples `wr_idx` is `34 % 32 = 2` and `pre` is 5. What is `(2 - 5) % 32` in C?

In C, `%` takes the sign of the **dividend**: `-3 % 32 == -3`, not `29` (C11 6.5.5p6: truncation toward zero). `ring[-3]` is outside the array. Make the dividend non-negative before taking the remainder: `(wr_idx - pre + BUF_LEN) % BUF_LEN`. This is safe because `pre <= BUF_LEN`.
explanation_md:
**Bug.** `start = (wr_idx - pre) % BUF_LEN` assumes that `%` is the mathematical modulo. In C (since C99, C11 6.5.5p6) integer division truncates toward zero, so the remainder has the **sign of the dividend**: `(2 - 5) % 32 == -3`. Whenever the buffer has wrapped and `wr_idx < pre`, `start` is negative, and `ring[(start + i) % BUF_LEN]` reads `ring[-3]`, `ring[-2]`, `ring[-1]` before reaching valid slots. That is an out-of-bounds read (UB). On the target it returns whatever lies before `ring` in RAM; here UBSan's bounds check (and ASan) stop it.

It only shows up when the trigger falls in the first `pre - 1` slots after a wrap. The first trigger after power-up never hits it, because before the first wrap `wr_idx == stored >= pre`. That is why bench tests passed.

**Fix.** Add the buffer length before the remainder so that the dividend is never negative: `(wr_idx - pre + BUF_LEN) % BUF_LEN`. Since `0 <= pre <= BUF_LEN`, the dividend stays in `[0, 2*BUF_LEN)`. For power-of-two lengths, `(wr_idx - pre) & (BUF_LEN - 1)` also works on two's-complement targets, but MISRA C discourages bitwise operations on signed values; using unsigned indices throughout is cleaner.

**Complexity.** O(P) per snapshot, O(1) per logged sample, O(BUF_LEN) memory.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating `%` as a modulo for negative operands. Python's `%` *is* floored; C's is not. This bites people who prototype in Python or MATLAB.
- "Fixing" with `abs(wr_idx - pre) % BUF_LEN`. It is non-negative but the wrong slot (`|-3| = 3` instead of `29`).
- Changing the type of `start` to `unsigned` without the `+ BUF_LEN`. `(unsigned)-3 % 32` is `29` only because 32 divides 2^32; with a length of 30 it silently gives the wrong slot.
- Forgetting to clamp `pre` to `stored` before power-up has filled the buffer (garbage or zeros from unwritten slots).

**Interview follow-ups**
- Re-implement the logger with free-running `uint32_t` write counters (as in a UART FIFO): `start = (wr - pre) & (N - 1)`. Why does unsigned arithmetic make the negative case disappear?
- The trigger is raised in an ISR while the logger task may be in the middle of `log_sample`. How do you make the snapshot consistent? (Freeze the write index first; double-buffer the snapshot.)
- Add **post-trigger** capture: keep logging `Q` more samples after the trigger, then freeze `P + Q` samples. How large must the buffer be?
- What does `-7 / 2` and `-7 % 2` give in C89 versus C99 and later? (C89 left the rounding direction implementation-defined.)
